title: Birbal and the pot of rice.
lines: Long ago in India there was a powerful emperor.
His name was Akbar.
He lived in a big palace with towers and gardens.
And he had a very clever friend, who always gave him advice.
That friend's name was Birbal.
Birbal was so clever that he could solve any problem.
One cold winter's evening Akbar said: It's so cold!
I don't think anyone can stand in the icy water of the lake for a whole night.
Whoever can do it will get a thousand gold coins from me!
A poor man heard that.
He needed money for his family.
I'll do it, he said.
That night the man stepped into the icy lake.
Brrr!
The water came up to his tummy.
His teeth chattered.
But he stayed standing.
All night long.
Far away, on the palace wall, a little lamp was burning.
The man looked at that little light all night long and thought of his family.
The next morning he came out of the water.
He was cold, but he had done it!
He went to the emperor.
I stood in the lake all night.
Akbar asked: How did you manage that?
I looked at the little lamp on the palace wall, said the man.
Akbar frowned.
Aha!
Then you kept yourself warm with the light of my lamp.
That doesn't count.
You get no gold!
The poor man went away sadly.
Birbal had heard everything.
He didn't think it was fair.
That afternoon Birbal didn't come to the palace.
Akbar waited and waited.
Where is Birbal?
He sent a messenger.
The messenger came back: Birbal says he'll come as soon as his khichdi is ready.
Khichdi is a dish of rice and lentils.
Akbar waited another hour.
Still no Birbal.
Then Akbar went to look himself.
And what did he see?
Birbal was sitting in his garden.
He had made a very small fire on the ground.
And the pot of rice was hanging very high, three metres up, from a branch of a tree.
Birbal!
shouted Akbar.
Your rice will never get warm like that!
That little fire is much too far away!
Birbal smiled.
Your Majesty, if a little lamp far away can warm a man in an icy lake, then surely my little fire can cook my rice?
Akbar was quiet for a moment.
Then he began to laugh.
Ha ha ha!
You're right, Birbal.
I wasn't fair.
The poor man got his thousand gold coins after all.
And Akbar and Birbal ate a tasty, warm khichdi together.
Cooked on an ordinary fire, of course.
